title: Old main-sequence M dwarfs in TESS 2-minute data with the corotation-to-stellar radius ratio of young CPV hosts have 2 CPVs where the contraction-only model predicts 8.9
abstract: Complex periodic variables (CPVs) are young, rapidly rotating M dwarfs with sharp dips at the rotation period. An earlier result found that x = R_cor/R* (BHAC15 contraction radii) explains the age decline of the CPV rate in 1-750 Myr BANYAN Sigma members with no extra age term. That model predicts that old main-sequence M dwarfs at P = 3-5 h, which have the same x as young CPV hosts, are CPVs at the young rate. We tested this prediction. We froze the model (fitted to 858 young members of the TESS sector 56-107 sample) and applied it to old main-sequence rapid rotators of that sample and of a new sample: 39,130 red dwarfs with 2-minute data only in sectors 1-55, which we processed with the same pipeline and labelled blind (sensitivity 0.86 relative to the source labels on 150 mixed-in calibration stars). The model predicts 8.9 CPVs (95% interval 6.1-12.6) among 386 main-sequence rapid rotators; we observe 2 (p = 0.013). At fixed x, the main-sequence rate is 0.23 (0.04-0.74) times the young rate. All 12 variants give a deficit (p = 0.003-0.031, except p = 0.15 for a strict dMG < 0 cut). The new sample also has fewer young CPVs than predicted, probably because known CPVs were re-observed after sector 55; with a free normalisation for the new sample the factor is 0.32 (0.05-1.05, p = 0.07), or 0.18 (p = 0.03) without one probable eclipsing binary. Inside the groups the model still works (35-60 Myr: 15 observed, 13.4 predicted). We report one near-main-sequence CPV candidate, TIC 248394276 (P = 3.57 h, 54 pc). Thus x is probably necessary but not sufficient, and a second property that declines after a few hundred Myr is also necessary. Limitations: moderate significance; one automated vetter; selection of the new sample; model extrapolation to P < 0.2 d; no spectra.
